name: Gum depigmentation
lead: Gum depigmentation is a cosmetic periodontal procedure that lightens dark, melanin-pigmented gums, using a scalpel, laser or chemical methods.[1] People have it done so that the gum line looks pink and even when they smile, which a 2026 review notes matters particularly for people with a high smile line who show a lot of gum.[16]

Wikipedia notes that gum pigmentation is mainly linked to genetics and tobacco smoking (smoker's melanosis), with melanin made by melanocytes in the basal layer of the gum.[1] A 2018 review describes pigmented gums as an esthetic matter that can also carry psychological negativity for the person, and notes that a wide range of techniques exists.[11]

Published research includes several systematic reviews and a growing set of randomized trials, mostly small, comparing scalpel surgery, diode, CO2, Er:YAG and Er,Cr:YSGG lasers, cryosurgery, microsurgery, bur-based methods, microneedling and injected vitamin C.[2][3][5][12][13][15][16]
infobox: Scalpel, laser, cryosurgery, bur, microneedling, injected vitamin C[1][6][13][15][16]

paras: Gum colour comes from melanin made by melanocytes in the basal layer of the gum epithelium. Wikipedia attributes pigmentation mainly to genetics and to tobacco smoking, which causes smoker's melanosis.[1] Physiological, ethnicity-related pigmentation is common and is treated for how it looks.[12][18]
For smokers, Wikipedia cites a study in which most patients had lost the pigmentation about three months after quitting.[1]

Wikipedia describes laser ablation of melanin-producing cells, scalpel removal of the pigmented layer by a periodontist or oral surgeon, and chemical methods that it says are used less today because of possible side effects.[1] Laser-treated gums heal by secondary intention.[1]

A 2014 systematic review listed bur abrasion, scalpel surgery, cryosurgery, electrosurgery, gingival grafts and lasers as the main options.[13] Lasers reported include CO2, diode, Nd:YAG, Er:YAG and Er,Cr:YSGG types.[14] Newer approaches under study include microneedling with topical agents and injected or topical vitamin C, which is of interest for its role in inhibiting melanin production.[6][7][8][16]

Wikipedia reports that laser treatment gives lighter, more uniform gum colour, that scalpel removal takes longer to heal, and that one Er,Cr:YSGG laser study showed no re-pigmentation at six months; the article is flagged for disputed neutrality and weak sourcing.[1]

Repigmentation is the main long-term question. The 2014 review, based mainly on case reports across 61 publications, found a wide range of recurrence rates between methods and reported low rates for cryosurgery (0.32 percent), electrosurgery (0.74 percent) and laser (1.16 percent).[13] A 2018 review reported that cryosurgery followed by lasers had been described as giving better esthetic results with lower recurrence, while calling for randomized longitudinal trials.[11] A randomized multicenter trial compared the longevity of results after diode, CO2 and Er:YAG laser depigmentation.[22]

For Er:YAG, a literature review found safe, effective depigmentation with significant esthetic improvement, while noting that studies use very different laser settings and different criteria for recurrence.[14]

The 2019 meta-analysis of 25 studies (17 randomized) found laser ablation and surgical stripping did not differ significantly for recurrence or depigmentation achieved, but laser was associated with significantly less postoperative pain.[12] Researchers have also studied topical argan oil, and coenzyme Q10 with vitamin C, as aids to healing after depigmentation.[9][10]

The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis included 25 human trials, mostly of lasers with scalpel surgery as the control; most found no difference between methods, and the meta-analysis showed no significant difference in recurrence (P = 0.75) or depigmentation (P = 0.23) between laser and scalpel, with less pain after laser.[12]

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies compared cryosurgery with laser, blade and abrasion for physiological gingival pigmentation; its abstract reports that laser and scalpel treatments had better therapeutic outcomes than cryosurgery.[15] A 2026 review of eight studies examined vitamin C as a stand-alone or combined treatment.[16]

Randomized trials include a split-mouth comparison of 940 nm ablative and 445 nm non-ablative laser depigmentation in 30 participants aged 18 to 35,[17] a 42-patient trial of injected vitamin C against surgical depigmentation in ethnicity-related hyperpigmentation,[18] a split-mouth vitamin C versus scalpel trial,[19] a split-mouth trial of a ceramic trimming bur,[20] and a comparison of Er,Cr:YSGG laser with surgical stripping with 12 months of follow-up.[21]

Registered trials include a 40-patient comparison of surgical stripping with an Er,Cr:YSGG laser,[2] comparisons of microsurgery with diode laser or conventional scalpel techniques,[3][4] a test of ceramic trimming burs against scalpel,[5] and ongoing trials of microneedling with silymarin or platelet-rich plasma and of vitamin C or glutathione.[6][7][8]

timeline.event: Systematic review of 61 publications compares recurrence across depigmentation methods.[13]
Randomized comparison of Er,Cr:YSGG laser and surgical stripping with 12-month follow-up published.[21]
Meta-analysis of 25 trials finds no significant difference in recurrence between laser and scalpel.[12]

card.summary: Dentist-performed lightening of dark gums by scalpel, laser or chemicals, backed so far by small comparison trials.
card.note: Evidence is small trials; pigment recurrence is reported inconsistently.

quick.overview:
Gum depigmentation lightens gums that are dark because of melanin, whether from genetics or smoking. It is done as a cosmetic dental procedure.

Most published trials are small and compare one technique against another rather than against no treatment.
quick.mechanism: Pigmented surface tissue is removed or ablated by scalpel, laser or chemical agents, and the gum heals with new, lighter tissue.
quick.risks: Wikipedia notes a longer recovery after scalpel surgery and possible side effects from chemical methods. Gums heal by secondary intention after laser treatment.

chain: Pigmented surface layer of the gum is removed or ablated
Gum heals with lighter, pinker tissue
More even gum colour when smiling
angle.text: Gum depigmentation changes the colour of the gum tissue itself, which people use to make the smile look cleaner and more uniform. It is performed by a dentist, periodontist or oral surgeon.[1]
